statement: On a 7 by 7 board, rows are numbered 1 to 7 from the top and columns 1 to 7 from the left. A frog sits in row 2, column 3. Each jump takes it exactly 2 squares left, right, up or down, staying on the board. How many squares can it reach, including its starting square?

choices.misconception: I assumed that by jumping around for long enough the frog could get everywhere.
I coloured the board like a chessboard and thought the frog could reach every square of its starting colour.
I counted the squares whose row and column are both odd, as if the frog had started in a corner.
I thought the frog could only reach squares whose row and column are both even, like its starting row.

hints: What happens to the row number when the frog jumps up or down?
A jump of 2 never changes whether the row number is odd or even, and the same is true for the column number. Colour each square by the pair (row odd or even, column odd or even).
The row stays even (2, 4 or 6) and the column stays odd (1, 3, 5 or 7). Every such square can be reached, so count 3 rows times 4 columns.

solutions.reliable: A jump of 2 squares up or down changes the row number by 2, so an even row stays even. A jump left or right changes the column number by 2, so an odd column stays odd. The frog starts in row 2 (even) and column 3 (odd), so it can only land in rows 2, 4, 6 and columns 1, 3, 5, 7. It can reach all of them by moving along the rows and columns in steps of 2. That is 3 x 4 = 12 squares. The transferable idea: when a move always changes a coordinate by 2, colour by odd and even coordinates, which splits the board into four classes, not two.
solutions.elegant: Four colours, one for each combination of odd or even row and odd or even column, split the board into classes of 16, 12, 12 and 9 squares. The frog never leaves its class, and the start is in a class of size 12.

whyOnTest: A colouring argument: the right colouring for jumps of 2 uses four colours, and the familiar chessboard colouring overcounts.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
